one_liner: Header-only C++ QP solver (ProxQP) on Eigen; 3.5-18x lower shifted-geomean solve time than OSQP on random QPs.
what_it_does: Solves convex quadratic programs: min 1/2 x'Hx + g'x subject to equalities Ax = b and inequalities l <= Cx <= u. Dense and sparse backends share one API: build `proxqp::dense::QP<T>` or `proxqp::sparse::QP<T, I>` from the problem dimensions, call `init(H, g, A, b, C, l, u)`, then `solve()`, and use `update(...)` for warm-started re-solves; results land in `qp.results`. Extras include dedicated box constraints (dense backend), solving the closest feasible problem when the QP is primal infeasible, nonconvex QPs through eigenvalue-based regularization, batches of QPs solved in parallel, and QPLayer for differentiating through a QP in PyTorch. Python and Julia bindings are provided, and CVXPY, CasADi and qpsolvers can call it as a backend.
how_it_is_fast: ProxQP is a proximal method of multipliers. Each outer step minimizes a primal-dual augmented Lagrangian merit function with a semismooth Newton method, and penalty parameters follow a BCL (bound-constrained Lagrangian) update rule. When penalties or the active set change, the dense backend updates its LDL^T factorization with rank-r updates instead of refactorizing. It factors either the regularized KKT matrix (PrimalDualLDLT) or H + rho I + A'A/mu_eq (PrimalLDLT, quicker when constraints far outnumber variables), after Ruiz equilibration. Warm starts keep the factorization between solves, and the linear algebra is vectorized through SIMDe (AVX2/AVX-512) when built with -march=native; the paper benchmarks used AVX2.
when_to_use: Small to medium dense QPs, solved repeatedly. The docs recommend the dense backend below a few thousand variables or above 0.1 matrix density; robotics MPC and inverse dynamics (TSID) are typical.
High-accuracy solutions (1e-6 to 1e-9). In the independent qpbenchmark Maros-Meszaros run, ProxQP scored 5.9 vs OSQP's 16.1 runtime shifted geomean at 1e-9, with a 52.9% vs 26.1% success rate.
Sequences of closely related QPs (MPC, control loops): the default WARM_START_WITH_PREVIOUS_RESULT mode reuses the previous iterates and factorization.
Problems that may be infeasible, where the closest feasible solution is useful, and QP layers in PyTorch that need derivatives (QPLayer).
C++ code already built on Eigen, or Python users who want `pip`/`conda` installs and CVXPY/CasADi integration.
when_not_to_use: Hard sparse QPs when PIQP or QPALM is available. On qpbenchmark Maros-Meszaros, PIQP is fastest at every accuracy (1.0 vs ProxQP's 5.9-53.3) with a higher success rate, and QPALM's runtime shifted geomean (2.2-4.8) also beats ProxQP's.
Loose default-tolerance runs: on qpbenchmark default settings ProxQP's runtime shifted geomean is 53.3 vs OSQP's 12.7.
Larger sparse MPC. One user (issue #227, 9 states per stage) found OSQP about 1.7x faster at horizon 70+, although ProxQP was faster at horizon 25 (1.1 vs 1.6 ms).
Sparse problems whose sparsity pattern changes between solves: a sparse `update` only works for an identical pattern, otherwise you must build a new QP object.
Hard real-time loops that need a guaranteed allocation-free solve: issues #103 and #200 about memory allocations are still open, and which calls allocate is not documented.

integration.dependencies: Eigen >= 3.0.5; optional SIMDe (vectorization, on by default in the CMake build), OpenMP (parallel batch solves), nanobind and cereal (Python bindings), Matio (tests)
integration.min_toolchain: C++14 minimum (CMake enforces 14, README says C++14/17/20); defaults to C++17, which the install doc lists as required; CMake build
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS and Windows (CI plus pip, conda-forge and Homebrew packages); x86 AVX2/AVX-512 through SIMDe when compiled with -march=native; vectorization can be switched off for other CPUs
integration.thread_safety: not documented for one QP object; separate QPs can be solved in parallel through the OpenMP batch solver (solve_in_parallel) or from Python threads with solve_no_gil (dense backend)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it handles the same convex QP class as OSQP and can stand in for it as a CVXPY, CasADi or qpsolvers backend, but the native API, the problem layout (separate equality and inequality matrices) and the settings all differ

gotchas: SIMD speed needs the vectorized build (CMake target proxsuite::proxsuite-vectorized or -DPROXSUITE_VECTORIZE) plus -march=native in your own compile flags. The docs name the CMake switch inconsistently: BUILD_WITH_VECTORIZATION_SUPPORT in the install guide, BUILD_WITH_SIMD_SUPPORT in the API doc.

The default initial guess is WARM_START_WITH_PREVIOUS_RESULT, so a re-solve on the same object starts from the previous iterates, proximal parameters and factorization unless you change `settings.initial_guess`.

The dense backend picks PrimalDualLDLT or PrimalLDLT by a complexity heuristic, and PrimalLDLT is documented as less accurate. For very ill-conditioned problems at tight tolerances, undoing the Ruiz scaling can lose precision.
Issue #63, a termination problem on the Maros-Meszaros problem QGFRDXPN, is still open.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: PIQP and QPALM also beat OSQP in qpbenchmark, and PIQP is faster and more robust on hard sparse Maros-Meszaros problems at every accuracy, so prefer PIQP there. Pick ProxQP for small dense QPs re-solved with warm starts (robotics MPC, whole-body control), or when you need its box-constraint handling, closest-feasible solving, nonconvex regularization or QPLayer differentiation.
verified_claims_summary: The project's own proxqp_benchmark (dense backend, i7-11850H, compiler, flags and solver versions unstated) reports shifted geometric means at 1e-9 accuracy with ProxQP = 1.0: OSQP 18.2 on dense random QPs, 3.5 on random QPs of about 15% density, and 14.2 on Maros-Meszaros (108.5 at 1e-3). The independent qpbenchmark run (i7-6500U, proxqp 0.6.6 vs osqp 0.6.7.post0 called through qpsolvers) has ProxQP ahead of OSQP at high, mid and low accuracy (5.9 vs 16.1, 19.2 vs 51.9, 36.0 vs 52.8) but behind at default settings (53.3 vs 12.7).
